planting.note: Fall-sow for natural cold stratification, or divide an established rootstock, into moist woodland soil at pH 5-6 with a shrub, trellis, or fence for the vine to scramble over.

directions: A Caucasus and Black Sea woodland vine that is the source plant for Georgian 'ekala pkhali,' a walnut-garlic shoot salad from the Imereti and Guria regions. Harvest only the soft, thornless spring shoot tips in roughly 10 centimeter segments, much like asparagus; older growth turns woody and hooked with thorns and is not eaten. Give it understory shade or dappled light and a support to climb, since vines elongate several meters per season once established.
sources: Green Canvas Farms - Georgian Smilax Salad (Ekala)

planting.note: Plant corm offsets or suckers into an excavated, humus-rich swamp pit kept under 8-28 inches of standing or slow-moving water, with partial shade from surrounding canopy.

directions: A classic Pacific atoll staple grown in Kiribati and Tuvalu in excavated humus-rich swamp pits under standing water, propagated from corm offsets rather than seed. Partial shade from surrounding breadfruit or coconut canopy is traditional and reduces heat stress on the crop. Corms can reach 60 centimeters long and tens of kilograms at full maturity, though most growers harvest smaller cormels well before that point.
sources: Mendiondo et al. 2024, Food and Energy Security - Cyrtosperma merkusii paludiculture

planting.note: Direct-sow or transplant into consistently moist, organically rich soil at a woodland edge or damp meadow margin; afternoon shade is actively beneficial in hot climates, not just tolerated.

directions: This is the plant behind 'dock pudding,' a Yorkshire Lenten dish of young spring leaves cooked with nettle tops and oatmeal. It needs consistently moist, organically rich soil and thrives at woodland edges and damp meadow margins, declining quickly if the soil dries out. Part shade genuinely helps in warmer or drier summer climates rather than being a mere tolerance, making it a good fit for a partly shaded, moist garden bed.

planting.note: Sow as soon as seed is ripe, or divide an established clump, into fertile soil in full sun to half shade; give it room, since it spreads aggressively by root.

directions: Historically naturalized around European monasteries specifically as a cooked rhubarb substitute, with tart, lemony leaves cooked like spinach or rhubarb. Like true rhubarb and spinach it contains oxalic acid, so eat it in moderate portions rather than as a staple green. It spreads vigorously from roots and self-seeds freely, so give it room or contain it, and it tolerates woodland-edge and building-shade sites well.

planting.note: Sow fully ripe, ground-fallen fruit promptly, since unripe seed germinates poorly; site under 20-70 percent shade cloth or companion-tree canopy in humid, high-rainfall conditions.

directions: A Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, and Papua New Guinea agroforestry staple grown deliberately as a partial-shade tree that in turn shades understory crops like sugarcane and edible hibiscus. Collect only fully ripe, ground-fallen fruit, since unripe seed germinates poorly. The kernel is eaten as a snack or cooked into main dishes, and seedlings grow comparably well under 30 percent shade as in full sun, making this a genuine multi-story food-forest tree rather than a full-sun-only species.

planting.note: Plant the whole ripe fruit immediately after it falls, since seed viability lasts only a few weeks and it cannot tolerate drying; site in moist coastal or riverine lowland soil under rainforest canopy.

directions: One of the few genuinely shade-adapted nut trees, naturally dominating the understory layer beneath taller rainforest canopy across the Pacific and sometimes forming nearly pure stands, making it well suited to a multi-story tropical food forest. Seeds are toxic raw and must be boiled or roasted before eating, in the traditional Pacific Island fashion. Heavy, deep shade does reduce seed yield, so partial canopy cover rather than dense shade gives the best production.
sources: ResearchGate - The Tahitian Chestnut: A Neglected Multi-Purpose Tree from the Asia-Pacific Region
